extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in the cognitive/evolutionary theory of humor (academics, students, comedians, and general readers curious about why things are funny)
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing or producing a scholarly/popular book that explains humor from cognitive, evolutionary, and social perspectives — covering theory, evidence, examples, and implications for practice (e.g., comedy, AI).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain the evolutionary/function of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a plausible account of why humor exists (e.g., humor evolved as a 'bribe' to motivate debugging of heuristic errors; why mirth and laughter developed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page excerpts: 'Humor, we propose, evolved out of a computational problem...' and the nursery-rhyme metaphor: Mother Nature 'bribes the brain with pleasure' so it will 'do all the tedious debugging'—the book is judged on how convincing and well-supported this evolutionary story is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for the phenomenology of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe what humor feels like, what elicits it, and how it is expressed (mirth, laughter, affective components).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review text: the book 'go into the phenomenology of humor (i.e. what it is like, what elicits it, how it is expressed, etc.)' — evaluators expect clear treatment of the subjective experience and elicitors of humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive review and critique of existing theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey prior theories (e.g., incongruity, relief, superiority) and show where they succeed and fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple reviews praise/expect the authors to 'go through the various theories of humor that have been proposed and attempt to show how they are all wanting in some manner.' Book is judged on breadth and fairness of literature review and critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answer key explanatory questions (theory completeness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pose and respond to the central questions a theory of humor must address (the book mentions 'twenty questions' any theory would have to successfully answer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expectation: a theory should explicitly confront core challenges and offer answers; reviewers note the book 'asks twenty questions that they think any theory of humor would have to successfully answer.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a clear core mechanism (testable/process account)
rubrics_metrics.description: State a central, coherent mechanism for humor (e.g., detection/fixing of false beliefs, mirth as reward) that connects to cognitive processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors propose that 'we laugh when we notice a flaw in our reasoning' and focus on 'mirth' and 'covertly entered belief' — criterion: the mechanism should be clearly articulated and applied to examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Link humor to cognition and emotion (emotion as necessary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain the role of emotions (curiosity, puzzlement, surprise, insight, mirth) in cognition and in producing humor; argue whether emotion is necessary for cognition/humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review: authors 'claim such emotions as curiosity, puzzlement, surprise, and insight are key components' and 'emotion is necessary for cognition' — book evaluated on how well it integrates emotion and cognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle diverse humor types (puns, slapstick, irony, inside jokes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for a wide range of humor forms — one-liners, puns, slapstick, irony, inside jokes, social laughter — and explain why each elicits mirth under the theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers expect the theory to 'make sense of' many forms (examples cited include puns, pratfalls, Mr. Bean, one-liners) and to explain both simple and complex cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain social functions of humor and laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Address how humor/laughter serve social roles (solidarity, tension relief, sexual selection, signaling intelligence) and provide evidence or argumentation for these functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviews discuss sexual selection (women find men funnier), social laughter unrelated to humor, and 'humour as a proxy for intelligence' — book should engage these social accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical implications for performers and designers (comedians, AI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer insights that are useful for joke-writers/comedians or for engineering humor in machines (e.g., what to experiment with, what components are required for a humor-capable AGI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several reviews note usefulness for comedians and the book's final chapter about 'what is needed to program a machine to express and appreciate humor' — criterion: practical, if tentative, guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use illustrative examples and jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Include plentiful, varied examples and jokes to demonstrate theoretical points and to keep readers engaged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page notes the book is 'peppered with jokes' and reviewers cite many sample jokes; expectation is that examples concretely illustrate abstract claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly rigor and references
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate rigorous research practices: cite literature, engage counterarguments, and provide empirical/theoretical support where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers praise 'rigour of the author's research' and expect thorough bibliographic grounding and careful argumentation rather than unsupported speculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, readability, and concision
rubrics_metrics.description: Write clearly and accessibly (short, clear chapters, avoid excessive jargon) so both specialists and interested lay readers can follow the argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple reviewers warn the book can be 'a slog' or 'jargon filled' and one suggests 'start with chapter six' for casual readers — criterion: accessibility without sacrificing substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance theory and entertainment (avoid over-solicitous academic dryness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain an engaging tone (wit, good cheer) and balance dense theoretical material with entertaining prose and jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steven Pinker blurb: 'written with clarity, good cheer, and, of course, wit.' Reviews note the book is academic but 'peppered with jokes' — authors should avoid alienating readers with dryness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overpromising (honest scope of claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious in claims about practical achievements (e.g., programming a humor-capable robot); do not oversell conclusions beyond evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism: 'They are guilty of a bit of oversell... They do not even give an outline of what such a program would look like.' Authors should be realistic about limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish first-person vs third-person humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and explain differences between humor experienced from a first-person perspective and humor on third-person targets/characters, and the implications for theory and performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers highlight this as 'particularly useful to comedians' — book should articulate perspective distinctions and their comedic consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for cultural/contextual and in-group effects (inside jokes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Address how cultural knowledge, shared context, and inside jokes affect humor reception and when exclusivity undermines comedic value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer argues 'inside jokes are the pinnacle of pretension' and that jokes 'should be accessible' — criterion: theory and advice should consider cultural specificity and inclusivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain why explanation often spoils a joke
rubrics_metrics.description: Handle meta-effects like why 'nothing kills a joke quite like having it explained to you' and describe constraints on explicating punchlines without destroying humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several reviewers observe that explaining jokes kills them; the theory must respect how explanation interacts with mirth and timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish empirical vs conceptual claims and address objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly separate speculative conceptual claims from empirically-supported claims and engage known objections or counterexamples in detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviews note many objections and a long chapter addressing them; book should transparently handle counterarguments (e.g., critiques of 'covertly entered belief').

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide structure and usable organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize material into manageable, intelligible chapters/sections (readers praised 'short chapters' and clear introductions tied to illustrative jokes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One reviewer: 'short chapters clear, concise and intelligently introduced by a joke' — good structure helps comprehension and engagement.
